standard_text: Write and use equations that model linear relationships to make predictions, including interpolation and extrapolation, in real-world situations involving bivariate measurement data. Interpret the slope and y-intercept in context.

progression.narrative: This standard hands students a line of best fit in slope intercept form and asks them to interpret the slope as a rate and the y-intercept as a starting value, then to use the equation to predict by interpolation and extrapolation and to judge whether a prediction is reasonable. The on-grade skills climb from recognizing a linear association, to reading a given fitted line, to judging fit, to interpreting a modeling equation, and finally to predicting with it. Students who stall here usually cannot yet pull a per-unit rate out of an equation or substitute a value and compute. Intervention should rebuild grade 5 coordinate plotting and grade 6 expression evaluation first, then the grade 7 skills of finding a unit rate and reading points on a proportional graph, and only then return to lines of best fit.

steps.rationale: The entry judgment of the standard: decide whether a scatter plot's points suggest a linear association at all. A line is only a model worth fitting when the data trends steadily up or down, so students must see association before they draw or trust any line.

The spec's Below-Proficiency band hands students a line of best fit and asks what its slope and y-intercept mean in context. Reading a given line is the gentlest form of 'using' a straight-line model, so it sits just after recognizing that a line fits.

The heart of 'informally fit a straight line and assess the model fit': judge whether a proposed line is a good or poor fit by how close it passes to the points, balanced above and below. This is the standard's own language and its core reasoning.

The spec's Approaching band moves from a graphed line to a modeling EQUATION and asks students to interpret its slope (a rate) and intercept (a start) in context, including negative slopes read as per-unit decreases -- the on-grade form of reading the fitted model.

The spec's At-Proficiency band uses the equation to make predictions, distinguishing interpolation (inside the data) from extrapolation (beyond it). Once a line is fit and interpreted, substituting an x to predict a y is what the model is for.

The standard tops out at the spec's Above-Proficiency band: judge and justify whether a prediction is reasonable, catching extrapolation pushed past the data or past a real-world limit where the straight line stops being trustworthy.

skills.name: Plot and read ordered pairs in the first quadrant

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot a point (x, y) by moving right then up from the origin, and read the coordinates of a plotted point.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot the point (3, 5), how far right and how far up do you go from the origin?

skills.i_do_script: A point on a grid is an ordered pair (x, y), and the order is fixed: the first number is steps right along the x-axis, the second is steps up along the y-axis. Watch (3, 5): start at the origin, go 3 right, then 5 up, and mark the dot. Reading is the reverse: for a plotted dot I say its across value first, then its up value. Right 2 then up 6 is a different spot from right 6 then up 2, so the order matters every time.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the coordinates, moving up by the first number and across by the second
canonical_error.example: Plots (3, 5) by going 5 right and 3 up, landing where (5, 3) belongs
canonical_error.why: The student ignores the fixed order of an ordered pair. The first coordinate is always the horizontal distance and the second is always the vertical distance. Swapping them puts the point in the wrong place and scrambles the shape of any scatter plot built from the pairs.

skills.item_template: A single ordered pair, or a plotted dot described in words. Student plots the point or reads its coordinates. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: To plot (4, 7), how many units right and how many up?
sample_items.answer: 4 right, 7 up

sample_items.stem: A dot is 6 right and 2 up from the origin. What are its coordinates?
In (x, y), which comes first, the across value or the up value?
sample_items.answer: The across value (x)

sample_items.stem: Where does the point (0, 9) sit?
sample_items.answer: On the y-axis, 9 units up

sample_items.stem: To plot (5, 1), how many units right and how many up?
sample_items.answer: 5 right, 1 up

sample_items.stem: A dot is 3 right and 3 up. What are its coordinates?
Where does the point (8, 0) sit?
sample_items.answer: On the x-axis, 8 units right

sample_items.stem: Are (2, 6) and (6, 2) the same point?
sample_items.answer: No, they are two different points

redirect_script.stop: Which number goes across and which goes up?
redirect_script.prompt: Read the pair left to right: the first number is steps right along the bottom, the second is steps up. Mark both orders on the grid, right 2 up 6 and right 6 up 2, and see that they land on two different dots.
redirect_script.praise: You moved across first, then up. That is the ordered pair read correctly.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that give a point's horizontal then vertical position.
The horizontal number line; the first coordinate is measured along it.
The vertical number line; the second coordinate is measured along it.
The point (0, 0) where the two axes cross.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 5 coordinate graphing with a labeled first-quadrant grid (across first, then up).

worked_example_script.text: On one grid, mark dot A at right 2, up 6 and dot B at right 6, up 2. Same two numbers, two different spots.
Which dot is the point (2, 6)? How do you know?
The first number, 2, is the across move and the second, 6, is the up move, so dot A is (2, 6). The order decides which spot the pair names.
If a student goes 6 right and 2 up for (2, 6), ask which number is written first. That one is the across move.
Your turn: plot (7, 3) and tell me the across move and the up move.

skills.name: Evaluate an expression for a given value of the variable

prerequisite_skill.description: Substitute a number for the variable in an expression like 4x + 3 and compute, multiplying before adding.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What is the value of 3x + 2 when x = 4?

skills.i_do_script: An expression like 4x + 3 is a recipe waiting for a number. Watch me evaluate it when x = 5: picture 4 bags with 5 counters in each bag, plus 3 loose counters. The 4x means 4 groups of x, so I multiply first: 4 times 5 is 20. Then I add the 3 loose counters: 20 + 3 = 23. Substitute the number for the letter, multiply before you add, and the expression turns into one value.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds before multiplying, or glues the substituted digit onto the coefficient
canonical_error.example: For 4x + 3 with x = 5, computes 4 times (5 + 3) = 32, or writes 45 + 3 = 48
canonical_error.why: The student ignores that 4x means 4 times x and that multiplication happens before addition. The bags picture fixes it: the 3 loose counters are not inside the bags, so they are added after the bags are counted.

skills.item_template: A one-variable expression with one operation on x plus or minus a constant, and a whole-number value for x. Student evaluates. Short response fluency bank, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: Evaluate 4x + 3 when x = 5.
Evaluate 2x + 9 when x = 6.
Evaluate 5x - 4 when x = 3.
Evaluate 10 - 2x when x = 4.
Evaluate 3x + 7 when x = 0.
Evaluate 6x when x = 7.
Evaluate x/2 + 1 when x = 8.
Evaluate 4x + 50 when x = 10.

redirect_script.stop: What does 4x mean: 4 plus x, or 4 groups of x?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw the bags: 4x is 4 bags of x counters, and the constant is loose counters outside the bags. Count the bags first (multiply), then add the loose ones.
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied first and added the constant after. That is exactly the order the expression asks for.

vocabulary.definition: A letter that stands for a number, like the x in 4x + 3.
Replace the variable with a number and compute the value.
The number multiplying the variable; in 4x the coefficient is 4.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 6 expressions with a bags-and-counters model (a coefficient as groups of the variable).

worked_example_script.text: Draw 4 bags labeled x and 3 loose counters next to them. Write 4x + 3 underneath.
If each bag holds 5 counters, how many counters are in the bags? How many in all?
4 bags of 5 is 20 counters, plus the 3 loose ones is 23. So 4x + 3 = 23 when x = 5. Multiply the groups first, then add what is outside them.
If a student gets 32, they added 5 + 3 first. Point at the picture: are the loose counters inside the bags?
Your turn: use the bags to evaluate 3x + 2 when x = 6.

skills.name: Find and interpret the unit rate in a proportional relationship

prerequisite_skill.description: Compute a unit rate from a table, description, or equation y = kx, and say what it means per one unit.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Apples cost 6 dollars for 3 pounds. What is the cost per pound?

skills.i_do_script: A unit rate answers the question, how much for just one? Watch: apples cost 6 dollars for 3 pounds. I divide the y amount by the x amount, 6 divided by 3, so the unit rate is 2 dollars per pound. In an equation like y = 5x for money earned (y) after x hours, the 5 is the unit rate: 5 dollars for each 1 hour. Say a unit rate with both units and the word per: 2 dollars per pound, 5 dollars per hour. The rate is always the y amount for exactly one x.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides in the wrong order, computing x over y instead of y over x
canonical_error.example: For 6 dollars and 3 pounds writes 3/6 = 0.5 and says apples cost 50 cents per pound
canonical_error.why: A unit rate is the y amount for one x, so the y goes on top. Dividing the other way answers a different question, pounds per dollar. A quick sense check catches it: 6 dollars spread over 3 pounds must be more than 1 dollar each.

skills.item_template: A proportional situation given as a description, a small table, or an equation y = kx. Student finds the unit rate or interprets what it means per one unit. Short response or multiple choice, no calculator.

sample_items.stem: Granola costs 12 dollars for 4 pounds. What is the cost per pound?
sample_items.answer: 3 dollars per pound

sample_items.stem: A car goes 180 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. What is its rate in miles per hour?
sample_items.answer: 60 miles per hour

sample_items.stem: The equation y = 5x gives dollars earned (y) after x hours. What is the unit rate?
sample_items.answer: 5 dollars per hour

sample_items.stem: In y = 8x, where x is tickets and y is total cost in dollars, what does the 8 mean?
sample_items.answer: Each ticket costs 8 dollars
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distractors: 'the total cost is 8 dollars' (reads the rate as a total), 'there are 8 tickets' (confuses rate with x), '8 tickets cost 1 dollar' (flips the rate)

sample_items.stem: A table shows x = 2, y = 10 and x = 5, y = 25. What is the unit rate?
sample_items.answer: 5 (y is 5 for each 1 x)

sample_items.stem: y = kx passes through the point (7, 21). What is k?
A printer prints 40 pages in 5 minutes. How many pages per minute?
sample_items.answer: 8 pages per minute

sample_items.stem: Which is the unit rate for 6 dollars per 3 pounds?
sample_items.answer: 2 dollars per pound
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distractors: '0.5 dollars per pound' (divided x by y), '6 dollars per pound' (used the total as the rate), '3 dollars per pound' (used the x amount as the rate)

redirect_script.stop: Which amount are you finding per ONE of?
redirect_script.prompt: Write the two quantities with labels, then divide the y amount by the x amount so you get the y for exactly one x. Check the sense: should one pound cost more or less than the whole bag?
redirect_script.praise: You divided to get the amount for one unit and said it with per. That is the unit rate.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of y for exactly one unit of x, like dollars per pound.
A relationship where y is always the same multiple of x, written y = kx.
The number k in y = kx; it equals the unit rate.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a bar for 6 dollars split into 3 equal parts, one part above each of 3 pound blocks.
If 3 pounds share the 6 dollars equally, how much lands on one pound?
Each part of the bar is 6 divided by 3, so 2 dollars sits over each pound. The unit rate is 2 dollars per pound, the cost of exactly one pound.
If a student writes 3/6 = 0.5, ask whether one pound of 6-dollars-for-3-pounds apples could really cost 50 cents. The picture shows 2 dollars over each pound.
Your turn: draw the bar and find the unit rate for 15 dollars for 5 pounds.

practice_problems.stem: 8 dollars for 2 pounds. Cost per pound?
practice_problems.answer: 4 dollars per pound

practice_problems.stem: In y = 6x, what is the unit rate?
A runner covers 21 miles in 3 hours at a steady pace. What is the unit rate in miles per hour?
practice_problems.answer: 7 miles per hour

practice_problems.stem: The equation y = 4x gives the cost y in dollars of x notebooks. What does the 4 mean in the story?
practice_problems.answer: Each notebook costs 4 dollars

practice_problems.stem: A table shows x = 3, y = 18 and x = 6, y = 36. Write the equation y = kx for this relationship.
practice_problems.answer: y = 6x

practice_problems.stem: Store A sells 5 pounds of rice for 10 dollars. Store B sells 4 pounds for 12 dollars. Find each unit rate. Which is the better buy?
practice_problems.answer: Store A is 2 dollars per pound and Store B is 3 dollars per pound, so Store A is the better buy

practice_problems.stem: A faucet fills 30 gallons in 4 minutes. Find the unit rate and use it to tell how much fills in 10 minutes.
practice_problems.answer: 7.5 gallons per minute, so 75 gallons in 10 minutes

practice_problems.stem: Maya found the unit rate for 12 dollars for 3 pounds of cherries. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She divided pounds by dollars, which gives pounds per dollar. The cost per pound is 12/3 = 4 dollars per pound. Sense check: 12 dollars over 3 pounds must be more than 1 dollar each.

activities.title: Share the Bar
activities.instructions:
1. Each pair gets a rate card like 6 dollars for 3 pounds.
2. Cut or fold a paper strip into the x number of equal parts (3 pounds means 3 parts).
3. Deal the money equally onto the parts and read the amount on ONE part. That is the unit rate.
4. Write the equation y = kx using the rate you found and check it against the card.
5. Repeat with 15 dollars for 5 pounds and 40 pages in 5 minutes. Say each time: this is the amount for one.

activities.title: Rate Round-Up
materials: Card deck: situation cards and unit rate cards
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each situation like 180 miles in 3 hours to its unit rate card like 60 miles per hour.
3. To claim a match, say the division out loud, y amount divided by x amount.
4. Two decoy cards show the division flipped; set them aside and explain why they answer the wrong question.

decoys: 0.5 dollars per pound for 6 dollars per 3 pounds
3 miles per hour for 180 miles in 3 hours

strategy_links.why: The shared bar makes 'the amount that lands on one unit' visible before the divide y by x rule is named.
The flipped division error is stable and baitable; finding and fixing it with a sense check confronts it directly.
Thinking aloud 'which amount am I finding per one of' makes the invisible choice of what goes on top audible.

questioning_prompts: Which quantity are you finding per one of?
What division gives the amount for exactly one unit?
Does your rate pass the sense check: should one unit be more or less than the total?
Where does the unit rate show up in the equation y = kx?
How would you say this rate with the word per?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides x by y and reports the flipped rate.
misconception_redirects.say: Deal the money onto the pound blocks: how much lands on one pound? The y amount goes on top because you want y for one x.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided the right way and the sense check confirmed it.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads the constant in y = kx as a total instead of a per-unit amount.
misconception_redirects.say: Plug in x = 1. The equation gives y = k, so k is what one unit costs, not the whole bill.
misconception_redirects.praise: You tested x = 1 and saw the rate is per one unit.

quick_checks.prompt: In y = 9x for dollars vs hours, what does 9 mean?
quick_checks.look_for: 9 dollars for each 1 hour, not a total of 9 dollars.

worked_solution.stem: Apples cost 6 dollars for 3 pounds. Find the unit rate.

steps.annotation: Label which amount is y and which is x.
Divide the y amount by the x amount to get y for one x.
Each pound gets 2 of the 6 dollars.
Say it with both units and the word per.

faded_example.stem: A car goes 150 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. Find the unit rate.

steps.annotation: Label the y amount and the x amount.
Divide miles by hours to get miles for one hour.
Compute the division.
State the rate with units and per.

sentence_starters: The unit rate is ___ per ___ because ___ divided by ___ is ___.
In y = ___x, the ___ tells me the amount of ___ for one ___.

skills.name: Interpret points on the graph of a proportional relationship

prerequisite_skill.description: Explain what a point (a, b) on a proportional graph means in the situation, including (0, 0) and the unit rate point (1, r).
prerequisite_skill.check_question: On a graph of a proportional relationship between hours and dollars earned, what does the point (1, 4) tell you?

skills.i_do_script: Every point on a graph is a fact about the situation, read in order: x first, then y. Watch a graph of hours worked (x) versus dollars earned (y) with the point (3, 12) on it: that point says 3 hours of work earns 12 dollars. Two points are special. The point (0, 0) says 0 hours earns 0 dollars, which is why a proportional graph starts at the origin. The point above x = 1, here (1, 4), gives the unit rate: 1 hour earns 4 dollars, so the whole line is built from 4 dollars per hour.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the meaning of the coordinates, reading (a, b) as if a were the y quantity
canonical_error.example: Reads the point (3, 12) on an hours versus dollars graph as 12 hours earning 3 dollars
canonical_error.why: The student forgets that the first coordinate always belongs to the x-axis quantity and the second to the y-axis quantity. Reading the axis labels first pins each number to its quantity, and the swapped reading usually fails a sense check.

skills.item_template: A proportional situation with labeled axes and one or two named points, described in text. Student states what a point means, identifies the unit rate point, or explains (0, 0). Short response or multiple choice.

sample_items.stem: A graph shows hours (x) vs dollars earned (y). What does the point (3, 12) mean?
sample_items.answer: 3 hours of work earns 12 dollars

sample_items.stem: On that same graph, what does the point (1, 4) tell you?
sample_items.answer: 1 hour earns 4 dollars; the unit rate is 4 dollars per hour

sample_items.stem: Why does the graph of a proportional relationship pass through (0, 0)?
sample_items.answer: 0 of the x quantity gives 0 of the y quantity, like 0 hours earning 0 dollars

sample_items.stem: A graph shows pounds (x) vs cost in dollars (y). Which statement matches the point (2, 8)?
sample_items.answer: 2 pounds cost 8 dollars
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distractors: '8 pounds cost 2 dollars' (coordinates swapped), '2 pounds cost 2 dollars' (ignores y), 'the cost is 8 dollars per pound' (reads a plain point as the unit rate)

sample_items.stem: On a gallons (x) vs miles (y) graph, the point (1, 30) is marked. What is the unit rate?
sample_items.answer: 30 miles per gallon

sample_items.stem: A graph of minutes (x) vs pages printed (y) passes through (5, 40). How many pages per minute is that?
sample_items.answer: 8 pages per minute

sample_items.stem: On a tickets (x) vs cost (y) graph, which point shows the cost of one ticket?
sample_items.answer: The point above x = 1, that is (1, r)
sample_items.distractor_logic: Distractors: '(0, 0)' (the start, not the rate), 'the highest point' (a total, not per one), 'any point where y = 1' (swaps the roles of x and y)

sample_items.stem: A graph shows weeks (x) vs dollars saved (y) with the point (4, 20). What does it mean, and what is the unit rate?
sample_items.answer: After 4 weeks, 20 dollars are saved; the rate is 5 dollars per week

redirect_script.stop: Which axis does each number in the point belong to?
redirect_script.prompt: Read the axis labels first, then the point in order: the first number is the x quantity, the second is the y quantity. Say the fact as a sentence and check that it makes sense in the story.
redirect_script.praise: You tied each coordinate to its axis and read the point as a fact about the situation.

vocabulary.definition: The point (0, 0); on a proportional graph it means none of x gives none of y.
The point (1, r) on a proportional graph; its y value is the unit rate.
The name of the quantity an axis measures, like hours or dollars.

worked_example_script.text: Sketch a line through the origin on axes labeled hours (x) and dollars earned (y). Mark the points (0, 0), (1, 4), and (3, 12).
Pick the point (3, 12). Which axis does the 3 belong to? Which axis does the 12 belong to?

The 3 sits on the hours axis and the 12 on the dollars axis, so the point says 3 hours earns 12 dollars. And (1, 4) says 1 hour earns 4 dollars, so 4 dollars per hour is the rate the whole line follows.
If a student says 12 hours earns 3 dollars, send them back to the axis labels: which axis did each number come from? Does 3 dollars for 12 hours make sense here?
Your turn: on the same graph, what would the point (2, 8) mean?

practice_problems.stem: On a graph of pounds (x) vs dollars (y), what does the point (1, 3) tell you?
practice_problems.answer: 1 pound costs 3 dollars; the unit rate is 3 dollars per pound

practice_problems.stem: What does the point (0, 0) mean on a graph of hours worked vs dollars earned?
practice_problems.answer: 0 hours worked earns 0 dollars

practice_problems.stem: A graph shows gallons (x) vs miles driven (y) and passes through (2, 60). What does that point mean?
practice_problems.answer: 2 gallons takes the car 60 miles

practice_problems.stem: On that gallons vs miles graph, what are the coordinates of the unit rate point, and what is the rate?
practice_problems.answer: (1, 30); the rate is 30 miles per gallon

practice_problems.stem: A graph of minutes (x) vs meters walked (y) passes through (4, 240). What does the point mean, and what is the unit rate?
practice_problems.answer: 4 minutes covers 240 meters; the rate is 60 meters per minute

practice_problems.stem: A proportional graph of tickets (x) vs cost (y) passes through (5, 45). Use the point to find the cost of one ticket.
practice_problems.answer: 45 / 5 = 9, so one ticket costs 9 dollars and the unit rate point is (1, 9)

practice_problems.stem: Two proportional graphs share the same axes, hours (x) vs dollars (y). Line A passes through (1, 6) and line B through (1, 4). What do those points tell you about the two jobs?
practice_problems.answer: Job A pays 6 dollars per hour and job B pays 4 dollars per hour, so line A is steeper and pays more per hour

practice_problems.stem: Leo read a point on a graph of hours (x) vs dollars earned (y). Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Leo wrote: working 12 hours earns 3 dollars.
practice_problems.answer: Leo swapped the coordinates. The first number belongs to the hours axis and the second to the dollars axis, so 3 hours earns 12 dollars. His reading also fails the sense check: 3 dollars for 12 hours of work is not this line.

activities.title: Walk the Line
materials: Large grid paper or taped floor grid
activities.instructions:
1. Label the axes from a situation card, like hours across and dollars up.
2. One partner places a sticky note at a point such as (3, 12); the other says the fact out loud: 3 hours earns 12 dollars.
3. Together find and mark the unit rate point above x = 1 and the origin, and say what each means.
4. Swap roles with a new card, like gallons vs miles through (2, 60).
5. Close with the rule: first number from the bottom axis, second number from the side axis.

activities.title: Point and Fact
materials: Card deck: point cards with axis labels, fact cards in words
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each point card, like (1, 4) on hours vs dollars, to its fact card, like 1 hour earns 4 dollars.
3. To claim a match, point to the axis each number belongs to.
4. Two decoy fact cards swap the coordinates; set them aside and explain the swap.

pairs.right: 1 hour earns 4 dollars, the unit rate

strategy_links.why: Placing and reading points on a physical grid makes 'first number across, second number up' concrete before points are read from printed graphs.
The coordinate swap is a clean, baitable error; find and fix with the axis labels corrects it.
Saying each point as a sentence to a partner forces the axis-to-number link to be spoken and checked aloud.

questioning_prompts: Which axis does the first number of the point belong to?
Say this point as a sentence about the situation.
Which point on the line shows the amount for exactly one unit?
Why must this graph pass through (0, 0)?
Does your reading of the point pass a sense check in the story?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps the coordinates when stating what a point means.
misconception_redirects.say: Touch the axis labels first: the first number came from the bottom axis, the second from the side axis. Now say the fact again.
misconception_redirects.praise: You anchored each number to its axis and the sentence came out right.

misconception_redirects.praise: You found the point above 1 and read the rate from it.

skills.name: Recognize when a scatter plot suggests a linear association
skills.i_do_script: Try the pencil test: lay a pencil across the plotted dots and tilt it -- if ONE tilt lets the whole set of dots hug the pencil, the data marches like a line; if no single tilt works, it doesn't. Before I ever draw a line, I ask whether the data even LOOKS like a line. I scan the points from left to right. If as x increases the y-values mostly climb, that is a positive linear association; if they mostly fall, that is a negative linear association; if they bounce up and down with no steady direction, there is NO linear association and a straight line would not model them. Watch (1,4), (2,7), (3,9), (4,12), (5,15): every step right, y climbs by about 3 -- a clear positive linear association, so a line is a reasonable model.

canonical_error.pattern: Decides there is a linear association by looking at only one or two points (or whether y is 'big'), instead of whether the whole set of points trends steadily up or steadily down.
canonical_error.example: For the scattered set (1,5), (2,12), (3,4), (4,15), (5,3) a student says 'yes, linear -- the numbers are large,' even though the points jump up and down with no consistent direction.
canonical_error.why: A linear association means the points, taken together, drift in one steady direction (up or down) so a straight line could summarize them. Judging from one point, or from how large the values are, ignores the overall trend -- a swarm with no direction has NO linear association no matter how big its numbers are.

skills.item_template: A small set of (x, y) points listed in text (or a short data table). Student decides whether the points suggest a linear association and, if so, its direction. Short response. (No figure -- data given as a list.)

sample_items.stem: Points: (1,4), (2,7), (3,9), (4,12), (5,15). Do these suggest a linear association? If so, which direction?
sample_items.answer: Yes -- a positive linear association (y climbs steadily as x grows).
Yes -- a negative linear association (y falls steadily as x grows).

sample_items.stem: Points: (1,5), (2,12), (3,4), (4,15), (5,3). Linear association?

skills.name: Interpret the slope and y-intercept of a given line of best fit in context
skills.i_do_script: When a line of best fit comes with its equation, my job is to say what the two numbers MEAN in the story -- and each number's meaning is how it behaves in the table. Take y = 4.5x + 50 for test score (y) versus hours studied (x). At x = 0 (no studying), the equation predicts 50 -- the y-intercept is the starting value. Each extra hour adds 4.5 more points -- the slope is a rate: how much y changes for each 1 more of x. Say both with units and direction: 'about 4.5 points per hour of studying' and 'about 50 points with no studying.' A negative slope reads as a drop: -1.75 means y falls 1.75 for each 1 more of x.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the roles of slope and y-intercept -- reads the y-intercept as the rate of change and the slope as the starting value.
canonical_error.example: For a line of best fit y = 4.5x + 50 (test score vs hours studied), the student says '50 means the score rises 50 points per hour' and '4.5 is the score with no studying,' reversing the two.
canonical_error.why: The slope is the amount y changes for each 1-unit increase in x -- a rate ('per hour'). The y-intercept is the value of y when x = 0 -- a starting amount. The student attaches the wrong role to each number, so both interpretations come out backward.

skills.name: Judge whether a proposed line is a good or poor fit to a scatter plot
skills.i_do_script: Once data trends like a line, I judge how WELL a proposed line fits by how close it passes to the points. A good fit threads the middle of the cloud: it stays near most points, with about as many points above the line as below it. A poor fit leaves the points far away, sits entirely above or below them, or runs the wrong direction. Watch the data (1,6), (2,6), (3,10), (4,10), (5,13) with the line y = 2x + 3: the points land at +1, -1, +1, -1, and 0 from the line -- all within 1 unit and balanced above and below, so it is a good fit. The line y = 2x + 8 leaves every point 4 to 6 units below it, so that line is a poor fit.

canonical_error.pattern: Calls a line a good fit if it passes through a couple of the points (often the first and last), instead of checking that it stays close to MOST points with about as many above as below.
canonical_error.example: For data (1,5), (2,6), (3,7), (4,8), (5,20), a student says y = 3.75x + 1.25 is a great fit 'because it goes right through (1,5) and (5,20),' even though it misses the four lower points by 3 to 9 units.
canonical_error.why: A good-fit line sits in the MIDDLE of the whole cloud, close to as many points as possible with roughly balanced amounts above and below. Touching two points -- especially an extreme one -- says nothing about the rest; the line can still be far from the bulk of the data, which is a poor fit.

skills.i_do_script: A modeling equation in y = mx + b form tells a story through its two numbers, and the slope can be negative. The slope is the per-unit rate of change -- how much y changes for each 1 more x -- and its SIGN tells the direction. Watch y = -4x + 50 for a plane's distance from a tower (y) after x minutes: the slope -4 means the plane moves 4 miles CLOSER each minute (down 4 per minute), and the intercept 50 means it starts 50 miles away at 0 minutes. skills.name: Use the equation to make predictions by interpolation and extrapolation
skills.i_do_script: Before the equation predicts anything, MY eye should: find x on the plot, ride up to the line, and read across -- about what y does the line promise? The substitution then confirms the eyeball number, and if the two disagree wildly, something got typed wrong. A line of best fit is a prediction machine: put in an x, get a predicted y. I substitute the known value for its matching variable, multiply by the slope FIRST, then add the intercept. Watch y = -2/3 x + 25 for flour (y) after x batches: to predict after 12 batches, y = -2/3(12) + 25 = -8 + 25 = 17 pounds. I also name the prediction: if the x is INSIDE the data range it is interpolation (usually safe); if it is BEYOND the range it is extrapolation (use with care). Twelve batches inside data that ran 1 to 20 is interpolation.

canonical_error.pattern: Substitutes the given number for the wrong variable, or breaks the order of operations -- adding before multiplying by the slope.
canonical_error.example: To predict flour after 12 batches with y = -2/3 x + 25, the student computes -2/3 + 25 x 12 = 299.33, or plugs 12 in for y, instead of y = -2/3(12) + 25 = 17.
canonical_error.why: In y = mx + b you substitute the KNOWN quantity for its matching variable (batches -> x), multiply by the slope FIRST, then add the intercept. Putting the value in the wrong variable, or adding the intercept before multiplying, produces a prediction that has nothing to do with the model.

skills.name: Judge and justify the reasonableness of predictions from a line of best fit
skills.i_do_script: The last step is judgment: not every number the equation spits out is trustworthy. A line of best fit is reliable NEAR the data it was built from. Predicting a little inside the data (interpolation) is usually safe; predicting far beyond it (extrapolation) assumes the straight line keeps going, which may not be true -- and some inputs are impossible in the story. Watch y = 203x - 11 for calories (y) burned walking x hours: at x = 10 the model predicts 203(10) - 11 = 2019 calories, but 10 hours is near the edge of what anyone walks in a day. At x = 30 the prediction is meaningless, because a day has no 30 walking hours and it is far past the data. So I justify each prediction with the data range and real-world sense.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats every prediction from the equation as equally reliable, ignoring that far extrapolation beyond the data (or past a real-world limit) may be unreasonable.
canonical_error.example: Using y = 203x - 11 for calories (y) vs hours walked (x), a student accepts the prediction for x = 30 hours as reliable, even though no one walks 30 hours in a day and the data only reached about 10.
canonical_error.why: A line of best fit is only trustworthy near the data it was built from. Predicting far outside that range (extrapolation) assumes the straight-line pattern keeps holding, which it often does not -- and some x-values are impossible in context. Reasonableness depends on whether the input is inside the data AND physically sensible, not just on the arithmetic.

worked_solution.answer: Not reasonable -- x = 30 is impossible and far beyond the data

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S4, interpreting the slope and y-intercept of a modeling equation in context, the workhorse on-grade skill the assessed items lean on. If they pass, push to S5 (predict by interpolation and extrapolation) and S6 (judge the reasonableness of predictions). If they fail, drop one grade: B1 checks whether the student can find and interpret a unit rate, and B2 checks whether they can read points on a proportional graph, the two grade 7 skills that slope and intercept reading grow out of. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (grade 5 coordinate plotting) and F2 (grade 6 expression evaluation) locate the gap further down. S1, S2, and S3 remain available to probe the standard's own association and fit groundwork.
